question: Does late stochastic-gradient motion in small underparameterized neural networks age like a glass, and does its characteristic timescale grow sublinearly with the network's waiting time?

key_findings.claim: The study defines aging through a two-time mean-squared displacement in parameter space rather than through training loss alone.
key_findings.evidence: For parameter vector theta and waiting time tw, the observable averages squared coordinate changes between tw and tw+t. A threshold crossing t-star at fixed displacement is then fit as t-star proportional to tw raised to mu, with mu below one designated subaging.

key_findings.claim: Three tiny tanh MLPs with similar parameter counts show a fast fitting phase followed by slow motion near low-lying loss regions despite very different cataloged landscape complexity.
key_findings.evidence: On 1,000 LJAT19 examples, one-, two-, and three-hidden-layer models have about 74, 69, and 72 parameters. Prior searches report roughly 10, 10^3, and 10^4 local minima respectively, yet all enter a loss region near 0.5 around step 10^3 and later evolve slowly.

key_findings.claim: Late-stage LJAT19 displacement is not time-translation invariant and becomes slower at larger waiting times, which the paper interprets as glassy aging.
key_findings.evidence: MSD curves for waiting times after about 10^3 steps shift systematically with tw for all three architectures, and their fixed-displacement characteristic times follow visually similar sublinear trends over a finite window.

key_findings.claim: A one-neuron-per-layer chain exhibits a similar loss/MSD pattern even though a short landscape search finds only one symmetry-related pair of minima.
key_findings.evidence: The minimal three-hidden-layer model contains about 15 parameters and still shows waiting-time-dependent displacement; the authors use it to argue that a large enumerated set of minima is not necessary for the observed phenomenology.

key_findings.claim: The MNIST experiments reproduce waiting-time dependence and yield a reported subaging exponent near 0.709 across the sampled underparameterized ratios.
key_findings.evidence: One- to three-hidden-layer models use roughly 4,000 parameters for 60,000 examples. For three-layer widths 7 through 17, threshold-crossing fits across selected alpha values give mean mu=0.709 with reported spread 0.017.

key_findings.claim: Hessian spectra move toward flatter, more positive local geometry during training while retaining some negative curvature under SGD.
key_findings.evidence: Boxplots for LJAT19 and MNIST show broad early spectra and late eigenvalues concentrated near zero with mostly positive outliers; the number of negative eigenvalues falls but does not vanish.

key_findings.claim: The data establish a descriptive parameter-space scaling regime, not that neural-network learning has the same mechanism or universality class as structural glass aging.
key_findings.evidence: Subaging is inferred from thresholded MSD fits over limited times; no glass-theory prediction derives mu, no alternative nonstationary SGD model is rejected, and the authors note a later-time regime with no standard glass analogue.

key_findings.claim: The claim of an architecture-robust or phase-wide exponent is much narrower than modern deep-learning practice.
key_findings.evidence: All networks are small fully connected tanh models trained with one fixed SGD recipe; the LJAT curves use a hand-drawn guide, and the MNIST phase is operationally restricted to alpha much less than one, accuracy below 0.99 by 10^6 steps, and widths 7-17.

method.core_idea: Borrow aging observables from glass physics to describe how SGD motion changes with the time at which a neural network is observed.
method.mechanism: Train underparameterized tanh MLPs with fixed-step minibatch SGD, record loss, accuracy, parameter displacement, gradients, and Hessian spectra, then fit the waiting-time dependence of the time needed to cross a chosen MSD level. Comparisons hold parameter count or P/N approximately fixed across depth.
assumptions: Euclidean displacement in raw parameter coordinates is a meaningful measure of functional training motion.
A power law fitted over the observed waiting-time window represents asymptotic aging.
The fixed displacement threshold lies in a regime where the fitted exponent is stable.
Holding parameter count or P/N roughly constant makes depth comparisons meaningful.
Small fully connected tanh networks reveal dynamics relevant to broader deep-learning systems.
Similarity to glassy observables indicates a useful shared statistical-mechanical mechanism.

techniques.role: Measures how late-stage SGD motion depends on both waiting time and elapsed time.
Converts families of MSD curves into a characteristic time t-star for power-law fitting.
Compares one-, two-, and three-layer MLPs at similar dimensionality.
Relates dynamics to minima counts obtained by prior basin-hopping and path-sampling work.
Characterizes local curvature changes from initialization to late training.
Averages characteristic times across 50 or 100 independently initialized runs.

evaluations.setting: LJAT19 four-class molecular-configuration task reduced to two inputs, N=1,000, with roughly 70-parameter MLPs of one to three hidden layers.
evaluations.metric: Loss, training accuracy, MSD at multiple waiting times, and threshold-crossing t-star.
evaluations.result: All depths show a fast/slow loss transition and waiting-time-dependent late motion with visually similar sublinear scaling.
evaluations.baseline: Architectures with matched parameter count but prior minima counts differing by orders of magnitude.

evaluations.setting: A minimal LJAT19 chain with one neuron in each of three hidden layers.
evaluations.result: Qualitatively similar slow aging appears despite only one pair of minima found by a nonexhaustive one-day search.

evaluations.setting: Full 60,000-example MNIST with approximately 4,000-parameter one-, two-, and three-layer MLPs.
evaluations.metric: Loss, accuracy, MSD, and characteristic-time scaling.
evaluations.result: The qualitative late dynamics and depth-insensitive subaging pattern recur on the more familiar dataset.

evaluations.setting: Three-hidden-layer MNIST networks across sampled P/N ratios in the operational underparameterized regime.
evaluations.metric: Least-squares exponent mu from t-star versus tw at Delta-star=10^-3.
evaluations.result: The reported mean exponent is 0.709 with spread 0.017 over the selected ratios.

evaluations.setting: Hessian and gradient diagnostics over training.
evaluations.metric: Eigenvalue distributions, Hessian trace, negative-curvature count, and gradient magnitude.
evaluations.result: Curvature concentrates near zero and gradients fluctuate around small values in the late phase, with deeper LJAT networks showing larger gradient fluctuations.

limitations: Raw parameter MSD is not invariant to neuron permutation, redundant reparameterization, or function-preserving coordinate transformations.
The networks are tiny fully connected tanh models; results do not cover ReLU, normalization, residual paths, convolutions, Transformers, or realistic parameter scales.
All main experiments use fixed-learning-rate vanilla SGD and a narrow set of batch sizes, so optimizer, schedule, momentum, and structured-noise dependence remain unknown.
Power laws are fitted over finite windows and selected displacement thresholds; LJAT architecture-independence is illustrated partly with hand-set guide lines.
The reported MNIST phase is an empirical subset of widths and accuracy conditions, not a proof of one universal exponent over all underparameterized networks.
Landscape minima searches are prior, architecture-specific, and nonexhaustive; the minimal-model search explicitly may have missed minima.
There is no connection from the aging exponent to test performance, convergence speed, optimizer choice, or an actionable training intervention.
The glass analogy is phenomenological and does not exclude simpler explanations from nonstationary gradient norms, curvature, or SGD noise.
failure_modes: A change in weight scale or permutation can inflate parameter MSD without a corresponding functional change.
A chosen Delta-star can cross transient plateaus rather than the purported asymptotic aging regime.
Averaging runs with different crossover times can create an apparently smooth power law.
Fixed learning rates can generate late diffusion or negative curvature that disappears under decay or adaptive optimization.
Accuracy-limited underparameterized networks may wander because they cannot fit the task, not because of a glass-like landscape mechanism.
The exponent can depend on activation, parameterization, dataset scaling, loss normalization, regularization, or batch noise that were held fixed.
reusable_insights: Use two-time observables to distinguish stationary late diffusion from optimization whose mobility changes with training age.
Pair loss curves with parameter, function, and representation-space motion; each captures a different notion of continued learning.
When claiming a universal exponent, preregister fit windows and thresholds and report sensitivity, goodness of fit, and competing functional forms.
Compare architectures with both parameter count and achieved function/accuracy matched, not one axis alone.
Track Hessian and gradient-noise evolution to relate phenomenological diffusion to an optimizer mechanism.
open_questions: Does subaging persist in function-space predictions, neural tangent kernels, or representation Gram matrices after quotienting parameter symmetries?
How do momentum, learning-rate decay, adaptive optimizers, batch size, and persistent SGD alter the exponent?
Can a dynamical mean-field theory derive mu and the crossover between the two reported late regimes?
Is the scaling present in modern residual, normalized, convolutional, or Transformer networks near their interpolation threshold?
Does an aging exponent predict generalization, grokking, flatness, or the value of continued training?
Which statistical test distinguishes a glassy aging law from nonstationary diffusion caused by ordinary gradient decay?

competitive_landscape.title: Comparing Dynamics: Deep Neural Networks versus Glassy Systems
competitive_landscape.difference: Baity-Jesi et al. first contrast underparameterized glass-like behavior with overparameterized bottom-of-landscape diffusion across networks; the target focuses on waiting-time scaling and reports a subaging exponent within the underparameterized side.

competitive_landscape.title: A jamming transition from under- to over-parametrization affects loss landscape and generalization
competitive_landscape.difference: Spigler et al. characterize a sharp fitting transition and three generalization regimes as parameter count crosses interpolation; the target stays below that transition and asks how the late SGD timescale depends on age.

competitive_landscape.title: Anomalous diffusion dynamics of learning in deep neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen et al. report a transition from superdiffusion to subdiffusion and attribute it to interactions with fractal-like loss geometry in ResNet/VGG settings; the target instead conditions displacement on waiting time and uses a glass-aging exponent in tiny underparameterized MLPs.

competitive_landscape.title: The Limiting Dynamics of SGD: Modified Loss, Phase Space Oscillations, and Anomalous Diffusion
competitive_landscape.difference: Kunin et al. derive a continuous-time finite-step SGD model and connect anomalous diffusion to modified loss, probability currents, Hessian structure, and hyperparameters with ImageNet evidence; the target offers an empirical aging law without a comparable optimizer mechanism.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: SGD in the underparameterized phase exhibits architecture-robust subaging, with MNIST governed by a unique exponent near 0.709 across the phase.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Waiting-time-dependent MSD curves recur in LJAT19 and MNIST ensembles, remain similar across small depth-matched architectures, and yield clustered threshold-crossing exponents over selected MNIST P/N values.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Applying a subaging observable adds a specific quantitative lens to earlier neural-network/glass comparisons. The universality language is premature: the result is coordinate-dependent, fit-window-sensitive, limited to tiny tanh MLPs and one SGD regime, and lacks a derived mechanism or link to learning quality.

reviewer_notes: Read all 16 extracted pages, including architecture/optimizer details, landscape caveats, Hessian and gradient appendices, and references. The audit distinguishes observed two-time scaling from a demonstrated glass universality class and flags raw parameter-space coordinate dependence. Direct primary antecedents and alternative SGD-dynamics accounts were checked on arXiv on 2026-08-23.
